Greedily
grēd´ĭ-lĭ
adv. (with eager craving; rendering Hebrew batsa, Greek ekchuno)
From greedy, Old English graedig. The adverb marks the manner of pursuit, which Scripture treats as damning independent of the object.

Biblical Definition

Greedily describes eager craving. Proverbs says of the wicked, “he coveteth greedily all the day long” (Pro 21:26), setting it against the righteous who giveth and spareth not. Jude condemns those who “ran greedily after the error of Balaam for reward” (Jud 11). Ezekiel indicts princes who “have greedily gained of thy neighbours by extortion” (Eze 22:12), and Isaiah calls the watchmen greedy dogs which can never have enough (Isa 56:11).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines greedily as with a keen appetite for food or drink; voraciously; ravenously; and with keen or ardent desire.

expand to see more

GREEDILY, adv. With a keen appetite for food or drink; voraciously; ravenously.

2. With keen or ardent desire.

Key Scripture

Pro 21:26 — "He coveteth greedily all the day long: but the righteous giveth and spareth not."

Jud 11 — "Woe unto them! for they have gone in the way of Cain, and ran greedily after the error of Balaam for reward, and perished in the gainsaying of Core."

Eze 22:12 — "In thee have they taken gifts to shed blood; thou hast taken usury and increase, and thou hast greedily gained of thy neighbours by extortion, and hast forgotten me, saith the Lord GOD."

Isa 56:11 — "Yea, they are greedy dogs which can never have enough, and they are shepherds that cannot understand: they all look to their own way, every one for his gain, from his quarter."

Modern Corruption

Ambition inside ministry is excused by its object, and Jude's charge against Balaam's imitators is entirely about the manner — they ran greedily, for reward.

expand to see more

Jude 11 names three failures and gives each a verb of motion: they have gone in the way of Cain, and ran greedily after the error of Balaam for reward, and perished in the gainsaying of Core. The Balaam clause is the one that lands on religious professionals. Balaam did not curse Israel; he could not. What he did was keep returning to the question because the fee was substantial, and Jude describes the imitators as running.

Isaiah 56:11 is the same charge aimed at shepherds: yea, they are greedy dogs which can never have enough, and they are shepherds that cannot understand: they all look to their own way, every one for his gain, from his quarter. The phrase can never have enough is the definition. Greed is not measured by what a man has taken but by the fact that no amount closes the account.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew batsa (H1214), to gain by violence, to be greedy of gain; nephesh azzah, a strong appetite; Greek ekchuno (G1632), to pour out, run riotously.

expand to see more

Hebrew batsa (H1214) — to gain unjustly, be greedy; Ezekiel 22:12, 27, Proverbs 1:19.

Hebrew avah (H183) — to desire greatly; Proverbs 21:26, he coveteth greedily all the day long.

Greek ekchuno (G1632) — to pour out, rush; Jude 11, ran greedily after the error of Balaam.

Usage

"“He coveteth greedily all the day long” — a settled occupation."

"“Ran greedily after the error of Balaam for reward” — the manner is the charge."

"“Greedy dogs which can never have enough” — the definition, applied to shepherds."
